items.title: I Don't Trust Visual Recordings Anymore. But One Day I Will Again
items.summary: Article URL: https://spectrum.ieee.org/fighting-back-against-deep-fakes Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50584429 Points: 10 # Comments: 1
items.content:
Hany Farid is a computer science professor at Dartmouth College, in Hanover, N.H.

In March of this year, a flurry of emails and text messages from a half dozen reporters around the world disrupted my quiet Saturday morning. An Iranian news agency had aired a week-old video of what appeared to be a U.S.-made Tomahawk missile hitting a school. News reports claimed that the strike killed more than 175 people, most of them children. The U.S. president and military denied responsibility. In the age of generative AI and all things deepfake , everyone—including me—was skeptical of the video’s authenticity.

I get this type of request a lot. For the past three decades, I’ve been developing mathematical and computational techniques to analyze and detect manipulation in digital media . Over this time, I think it’s fair to say that I, like most people, have approached visual recordings with a “presumption of authenticity”: If a skeptic claims that a recording is fake, the burden of proof is on them.

In today’s world of generative AI, however, I think we need to shift this stance to a “presumption of fake.” That is, the burden is now on the creator to prove that their content is real. While this new stance may seem unfair to legitimate creators, I think it both reflects reality and points to a future where we will once again be able to trust that most online media is what it appears to be.

Even last March, I was already tilting toward a presumption of fake. My initial response to the reporters was something along the lines of, “I am suspicious of the video because the quality is low, it emerged weeks after the bombing, and it is only being distributed by an Iranian news agency with a less-than-stellar record of accurate reporting.”

Given the potential implications—if the video was indeed real, however, I resigned myself to spending my Saturday morning analyzing it.

I first reasoned that if the Tomahawk missile was digitally added to each frame of the video without taking into consideration the camera motion, we might see a physically implausible missile path. So I aligned the video frames using a stationary background landmark as a reference. In the updated video, the missile did, in fact, move in a nearly linear trajectory. (See the yellow dots in the composite shown below.)

I next asked if the size (in pixels) of the missile in the video was plausible. Under some reasonable assumptions, I estimated that the missile in the video corresponded to a 6-meter Tomahawk at a distance of approximately 100 meters. The distance seemed plausible from the scene and was also consistent with the delay of 0.3 seconds from visible impact to the sound of impact, given that sound travels at 343 meters per second.

A composite photo composed of frames from a video of the Tomahawk strike reveals the missile’s trajectory. Hany Farid; Source: Mehr News

Despite the mounting evidence, though, I struggled to refine my answer for the reporters.

My skepticism was fueled by a recent study I worked on with colleagues at the University of California, Berkeley, that showed how hard it is to distinguish real from fake videos. Observers are now so suspicious of videos in general that they have trouble convincing themselves that a video is real.

But after a few more hours and a few more analyses with the missile video, I finally decided that it was authentic, and I gave the reporters my updated view.

This analysis marked a turning point for me. I realized I was just like the participants in our study: The lack of artifacts was not enough to readily convince me a video is real. I had flipped from a presumption of real to a presumption of fake.

When the visual record is no longer reliable, what can we do?

The types of forensic analyses that I routinely perform do not currently operate at internet scale and speed. But provenance signals can. These signals include content credentials and watermarks that are inserted or embedded at the time of creation or recording.

Credentials that follow the C2PA standard, for example, attach a cryptographically signed manifest to a photo or video at the moment of capture; this metadata records the device, the time and location of the recording, and any subsequent edits. Because the manifest is signed, any tampering with either the content or its history can be detected later by machine. Watermarks, like Google’s SynthID , embed an imperceptible signal directly into the pixels or audio samples that identifies the content’s origin.

Apple recently took these ideas a step further . On some of its newest iPhones, the camera sensor can cryptographically sign the raw pixel data as it’s captured. That signed data is then developed into a reference image saved alongside the normal, editable photo. Anyone can then compare the two and see exactly what, if anything, was changed.

These provenance signals are often criticized as being only a partial solution or vulnerable to attack. This is true if we think of them as mechanisms for catching bad actors. But that’s not what they’re supposed to do. Their purpose is to let good actors prove that their audiovisual recording is what it claims to be.

Provenance signals thus need not be adversary-proof. Instead, these signals are part of a new reality in which consumers, journalists, and the courts must adapt to a presumption of fakeness. If enough good actors adopt these mechanisms, they can begin to drown out bad actors. In other words, we have to switch from a model of “catch the bad actors” to “empower the good actors.”

This switch from trust to distrust of digital media has expanded to include routine video calls.

In September 2024, for example, Senator Ben Cardin (D-Md.), then chair of the Foreign Relations Committee, received a video meeting request from Dmytro Kuleba, who until a few weeks earlier had been Ukraine’s foreign minister. During the call, Cardin became suspicious when, out of character, Kuleba pressed him on whether the U.S. should allow Ukraine to fire long-range missiles into Russia . Cardin ended the call. Later, the State Department confirmed that Kuleba had never requested the meeting, and the Senate security office warned staff that foreign adversaries, possibly Russian, would likely try similar faked meetings again.

All it takes to conduct this type of impersonation is a face swap or avatar deepfake, along with voice conversion, both of which substitute the speaker’s face and voice for deepfaked versions in real time. These technologies are readily available in commercial products and open-source libraries and run on nothing more powerful than a modern laptop.

This video illustrates the current state of face-swap deepfakes.

Farid’s Company GetReal Shows How Real Deepfake Videos Look Today Your browser does not support the video tag. Firms that verify provenance have to move fast to detect real-time deepfakes . Hany Farid, GetReal

Unlike the Tomahawk video, which I could sit with for a morning analyzing frame by frame, a live video call offers no time for human analysis. On the other hand, real-time deepfakes pose new challenges for their creators: A fake video call has to be generated at around 24 frames per second to fool the eye into perceiving realistic motion. As a result, the deepfake-video-call software has to take shortcuts , such as simplifying faces and how they interact with their surroundings, and allowing some drift between audio and video or between video frames. The human eye doesn’t notice the shortcuts, but we can forensically expose them.

Provenance signals should eventually play a role here. Video-calling software could apply the same cryptographic signing to each frame of a live video stream that Apple now applies to still photographs. A face swap necessarily occurs between a speaker’s camera and the videoconferencing software, and so the software could verify in real time whether the frames it’s receiving were signed by a physical camera sensor or whether they were altered in transit. As before, the burden shifts from catching the impersonator to allowing real participants to prove they are who they claim to be.

For the first two decades of the digital revolution, forensic analysis—finding the telltale traces of manipulation—was enough to adjudicate most questions of authenticity. The AI revolution, however, has changed the scale and speed of manipulation beyond what forensics alone can handle. To believe a recording is real now, it must also carry a provenance signal from the point of recording. The two approaches work together, with provenance allowing good actors to be trusted, while forensic analyses root out the bad actors.

Hany Farid is a computer science professor at Dartmouth College, in Hanover, N.H. About 10 years ago, he randomly picked up a book in the library on the federal rules of evidence and was astonished to learn that courts made no distinction between photos from negatives and digital photos, even though the latter can be easily altered. “Digital photography was just getting started,” Farid says. “I realized this was really going to be a huge problem.” Since then digital photo forensics has become the focus of his research. He now frequently testifies in U.S. courts and advises law enforcement agencies. “All that from picking up a book,” he says.

items.title: Mamdani announces plan to close New York's Rikers Island jail by 2032
items.summary: Plans to shutter the troubled facility date back to 2019, when the city council first voted to close it but delays arose over where to place inmates.
items.content:
New York City's official overseeing the closure of the city's most notorious jail hopes a new plan from Mayor Zohran Mamdani will lead to "a moment of transformation" for how people are detained in the largest US city.

Mamdani on Friday unveiled a plan to close the Rikers Island complex by 2032, to build four new jails and drastically reduce the city's detainee population.

Plans to shutter the troubled facility date back to 2019, when the city council first voted to close it by this year. But plans have been delayed over the years in part due to the logistical difficulties over where to place inmates.

Dana Kaplan - who Mamdani appointed as the city's "Close Rikers Czar" told the BBC News channel on Friday that his latest proposal is not just about getting rid of a decrepit facility.

It is also a "generational opportunity" to "build a different type of detention system" and figure out how to detain people more appropriately, she said.

The Rikers Island jail complex is perched on a 413 acre (167 hectare) island between Queens and the Bronx, and has earned a variety of nicknames over the years because of its dilapidated conditions, including Gladiator School and Torture Island. The jail has housed a number of high-profile inmates awaiting trial, including Tupac Shakur, DMX and Harvey Weinstein.

It houses more than 6,500 inmates at a given time. Mamdani hopes to reduce that number to 4,100 - a goal that has been met with skepticism by the New York City correction officers' union.

"[B]uilding a new system that puts an arbitrary cap on the City's available jail beds is ill-conceived, irresponsible and jeopardizes the safety of all New Yorkers, including our Officers," NYC Correction Officers' Benevolent Association said in a statement. "The City cannot keep the jail population at around 4,100 without irresponsibly releasing individuals who committed violent felony charges."

"It's actually possible to have fewer people in jail in New York City - and that is what we should be planning for," she said.

The jail complex has long faced backlash over staffing shortages, crumbling conditions and inmate deaths in the facility, including nine this year. Legislation required the jail to be shuttered by 2027, but Mamdani blamed lags under former Mayor Eric Adams' administration as well as the Covid pandemic for the delays.

Last year, under Adams, a federal judge removed Rikers from the city's control, appointing an independent outside official to make decisions concerning the facility.

In an 88-page report released on Friday, Mamdani said Rikers was a product of "deteriorating infrastructure" and that officials had a "moral imperative" to close it.

New York City Council must approve the updated timeline, with members, including the city's speaker, indicating they support the plan.

Mamdani's office said the city would open up four new jails - one in Brooklyn by 2029, two in the Bronx and Queens by 2031 and one in Manhattan by 2032.

The mayor's office argues the new, smaller facilities will provide inmates "access to daylight, fresh air and clean space" leading to better outcomes for detainees. The facilities will be easier for families to access as well, as travel to the remote Rikers can take hours.

Mamdani said his administration would work to reduce the number of people being held in jail across New York City, including by offering alternative programmes to detention for some awaiting trial, by making it easier for families to post bail online and by trying to speed up the pretrial legal process.

He also wants to open up hundreds of beds in therapeutic housing units for prisoners with serious mental health issues.

Kaplan said Mamdani's administration had already opened 100 therapeutic beds at Bellevue Hospital in Manhattan, moving 100 people off of Rikers Island.

The proposal involves a large investments: $146m (£111m) for mental health and substance use treatment and vocational and education programming inside and outside the jails.

items.title: Libri digitali, FI insiste ma Meloni blinda il decreto con la fiducia
items.summary: Emendamento degli azzurri alla Camera: stop allo sconto al 50%, Mercoledì la tagliola. Ipotesi ristoro agli editori in legge di bilancio
items.content:
Il messaggio di Giorgia Meloni è già stato recapitato ai vertici del gruppo di FdI alla Camera: sul decreto scuola il governo porrà la fiducia. Infuriata con Stefania Craxi e col grosso di Forza Italia, la premier vuole archiviare in fretta la fragorosa spaccatura della maggioranza sui libri scolastici in digitale. Tutto va chiuso entro mercoledì, col voto finale dell’aula, dopo il pasticcio del Senato. Gli azzurri per ora insistono: ieri hanno protocollato in commissione Cultura tre emendamenti, uno soppressivo della norma sugli e-book così cara a Fratelli d’Italia, due per limitarne la portata. Pure i meloniani, con Fabio Rampelli , ne hanno presentato uno, che subordina l’adozione dei manuali in digitale, sia alle elementari che alle medie, al vaglio di una commissione tecnica, chiamata a valutare l’«impatto cognitivo» per i bambini. È un possibile compromesso, ma tutti gli emendamenti sono destinati a cadere: la commissione si riunirà lunedì e il giorno dopo dovrebbe andare in Aula senza mandato al relatore. Con la fiducia, tutte le proposte di modifica saranno stralciate. Gli azzurri pensano allora di riproporle con un ordine del giorno, che però non pone alcun vincolo all’esecutivo.

Dopo tre giorni di bordate e strappi, Antonio Tajani fa il pompiere: «Vedrete che alla fine si troverà un accordo». Lo stesso vicepremier fa capire che «si possono trovare delle formule che possano permettere di difendere un principio». Come l’ordine del giorno, appunto. Ma non è solo questione di principi: i forzisti sperano che sia previsto in manovra un ristoro per le case editrici. Trattative in corso. Whatsapp e chiamate tra Tajani e Meloni. Si vedrà. La premier, nelle conversazioni di queste ore con gli esponenti del suo partito, appare ancora estremamente irritata dal comportamento di FI a Palazzo Madama. Ce l’ha con la capogruppo Craxi, tratteggiata in privato come una politica «che pensa di vivere ancora nella Prima Repubblica», quando i partiti di maggioranza potevano «mandare sotto il governo senza conseguenze». Non è un caso che Ignazio La Russa ieri abbia evocato una «verifica» sulla tenuta della maggioranza. Il governo, dice il presidente del Senato, «non può cadere», ma «il clima dovrà essere verificato nei prossimi giorni».

Meloni teme la slavina, da qui alle elezioni, su altri provvedimenti. Dal reintegro dei medici no vax, a cui FI si oppone, alla legge più delicata, quella di bilancio, ostaggio dei partiti di maggioranza, che vogliono piazzare tutte le bandierine prima delle urne. Fosse per la premier — l’ha ripetuto anche in queste ore tribolate — si voterebbe subito. Anche perché ormai è chiaro che «così non si regge un anno».

È soprattutto la manovra a crucciare Meloni. È infastidita (eufemismo) non solo per i quasi 2mila emendamenti presentati dalle forze della sua coalizione. Ma soprattutto per il centinaio di emendamenti a cui stanno lavorando i suoi ministri. Quasi sempre «di FI e Lega». E senza seguire le indicazioni impartite sia dalla premier che dal ministro dell’Economia, Giancarlo Giorgetti : è dall’estate predicano calma e mal tollerano questi arrembaggi. Qualcuno non ha capito che se non si mette seriamente, alla svelta, un freno a queste scorrerie scombinate, è il ragionamento che fanno le alte sfere di FdI, a questo giro si rischia sul serio l’esercizio provvisorio. Si sono tenute anche riunioni in Senato, per capire come arrivare all’obiettivo, cioè il via libera finale entro capodanno. Ma i margini si fanno sempre più sottili. Mentre il metaforico piatto della bilancia per le urne anticipate, nella testa di Meloni, si fa sempre più pesante.

items.title: Guerra Ucraina - Russia, le news di oggi. Nuove esplosioni a Kiev: allerta per un attacco di droni. Trump: “Prima l’accordo, poi le garanzie di sicurezza”
items.summary: L'aeronautica ucraina segnala un drone a reazione diretto verso la capitale. Washington punta a un'intesa di pace entro l'inizio di gennaio. Macron denuncia l'aggressività di Mosca in Europa dopo gli incidenti in Polonia e Danimarca
items.content:
Nuova notte di allerta aerea a Kiev , dove sono state udite esplosioni per la minaccia di un attacco con droni russi. L'aeronautica militare ucraina ha segnalato anche un drone a reazione diretto verso la capitale , già colpita nelle ore precedenti da una serie di raid che hanno provocato morti, feriti e danni alle infrastrutture.

Intanto proseguono i tentativi diplomatici per mettere fine alla guerra. Il presidente Trump ha dichiarato che prima di discutere delle garanzie di sicurezza per l'Ucraina è necessario raggiungere un accordo di pace. Secondo il Financial Times , Washington punta a un'intesa tra Kiev e Mosca entro l'inizio di gennaio . Sul fronte europeo cresce invece la tensione dopo la violazione dello spazio aereo polacco da parte di missili e droni russi e l'espulsione di un diplomatico di Mosca dalla Danimarca. Il presidente francese Emmanuel Macron ha denunciato una nuova aggressività della Russia sul territorio europeo.

Zelensky: “Ponte di Kerch obiettivo lecito, Putin capisca cos'è la guerra”

Il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky ha affermato in una intervista alla Nbc che il ponte di Kerch in Crimea , è un obiettivo assolutamente legittimo per gli attacchi ucraini, poiché l'Ucraina sta solo reagendo all'aggressione russa e che non resterà certamente inerte. L'intervista è ripresa dalla Ukrainska Pravda. "La nostra regola è molto semplice: rispondiamo. Se attaccano le nostre infrastrutture energetiche, e questo è successo ripetutamente, stiamo cercando il modo di rispondere. La Russia deve capire cosa sia la guerra". I russi, ha detto ancora Zelensky, "ci attaccano da anni, distruggendo ponti (che molti ormai hanno dimenticato), ferrovie, ecc. Ovviamente, dovevamo rispondere, in particolare colpendo il ponte di Crimea. Questo è un obiettivo assolutamente legittimo per noi, perché hanno occupato la nostra Crimea. Hanno costruito questo ponte e hanno dichiarato che faceva parte della Russia". "Lui (il leader russo Vladimir Putin, ndr ) deve capire: questo ponte non reggerà. Sia ora, durante la guerra, sia più tardi, quando la guerra sarà finita. In ogni caso, sia diplomaticamente che militarmente, non accetteremo il fatto che i territori siano occupati da Putin e dai russi. Non accetteremo nemmeno una simile forma di militarizzazione, la militarizzazione del nostro territorio ucraino. Dopotutto, lui (Putin - ndr) usa questo ponte per trasferire quante più armi possibile. Questa sarà quindi la nostra risposta".

Raid russo su Zaporizhzhia, colpito un asilo nido Incendio scoppia anche in un appartamento vicino

“Il nemico ha attaccato Zaporizhzhia . Un asilo è stato colpito. A seguito dell'attacco, anche un appartamento in un edificio adiacente di cinque piani ha preso fuoco". È quanto si legge in un rapporto su Telegram del capo ad interim dell'amministrazione militare ucraina di Zaporizhzhia, Mykhailo Semikin, citato da Ukrinform .

Sale a 42 il bilancio dei feriti per l’attacco russo su Kryvyi Rih

Il bilancio delle vittime dell'attacco a Kryvyi Rih è salito a 42, tra cui quattro bambini. La notizia è stata diffusa su Telegram dal capo del Consiglio di Difesa di Kryvyi Rih, Oleksandr Vilkul, secondo quanto riportato da Ukrinform. "Alle 23:00 si contavano già 42 feriti, di cui quattro bambini. Una ragazza di 20 anni e un bambino di 7 anni sono deceduti", ha scritto. Secondo Vilkul, 27 persone versano in gravi condizioni. I medici stanno fornendo a loro e a tutti i feriti tutta l'assistenza necessaria. Secondo i dati preliminari, 23 edifici residenziali, un ospedale e alcune strutture commerciali hanno subito danni.

Kiev: “Allerta aerea nella capitale, sentite delle esplosioni”

“Un'allerta aerea è stata dichiarata in nottata a Kiev per la minaccia di un attacco aereo con droni. In città si sono udite delle esplosioni". Lo rende noto l'aeronautica militare ucraina che ha anche "segnalato un drone a reazione diretto verso Kiev". Lo riporta l' Ukrainska Pravda.

"Gli occupanti russi hanno attaccato in serata il centro di Kryvyi Rih con missili balistici, uccidendo una donna e un bambino di sette anni . Ventuno persone sono rimaste ferite". Lo hanno reso noto, scrive l'Ukrainska Pravda, il capo dell'amministrazione di Dnipropetrovsk, Oleksandr Ganzha, e Mykola Lukashuk, presidente del Consiglio regionale di Dnipropetrovsk. "Tra i feriti ci sono tre bambini, tra cui uno di 7 anni in gravi condizioni. Adesso si trova in ospedale e i medici stanno lottando per salvargli la vita", hanno aggiunto le fonti.

items.title: Re: Riemann
items.summary: Article URL: https://borretti.me/article/re-riemann Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50583982 Points: 165 # Comments: 156
items.content:
A fun thing about living in Australia is that most things happen overnight, so reading the news in the morning is like a gacha game . You pick up the phone and scroll through notifications of world-historic events: elections won, wars begun, models released, conjectures proven or refuted. Today’s pull was a Discord notification saying: “they proved riemann :/”.

This part of the announcement caught my attention (bold mine):

I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end , in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater .

It was my secret in my student days that my plans were for this problem in decades, which meant then that I tried to become familiar with all tools that I could possibly recognize in the problem when it was time. Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line. No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line . I had us on the line of combining two quite different ideas present in a toy setting, one of which was already new and shocking, making very simple one of the shadows of Riemann over which we mathematicians felt most triumph. I guided us to the right situation analogous to that toy setting, and then Claude began to leave me in awe .

Compare the above to Ayn Rand’s account of watching the launch of Apollo 11:

What we had seen, in naked essentials—but in reality, not in a work of art—was the concretized abstraction of man’s greatness.

The meaning of the sight lay in the fact that when those dark red wings of fire flared open, one knew that one was not looking at a normal occurrence, but at a cataclysm which, if unleashed by nature, would have wiped man out of existence—and one knew also that this cataclysm was planned, unleashed, and controlled by man, that this unimaginable power was ruled by his power and, obediently serving his purpose, was making way for a slender, rising craft. One knew that this spectacle was not the product of inanimate nature, like some aurora borealis, or of chance, or of luck, that it was unmistakably human—with “human,” for once, meaning grandeur —that a purpose and a long, sustained, disciplined effort had gone to achieve this series of moments, and that man was succeeding, succeeding, succeeding! For once, if only for seven minutes, the worst among those who saw it had to feel—not “How small is man by the side of the Grand Canyon!”—but “How great is man and how safe is nature when he conquers it!”

Rand’s essay says: how great is Man! How noble in reason, how infinite in faculty ! The Riemann announcement reads like a suicide note, or like the farewell message of a terminally-ill person who’s about to undergo euthanasia: “I shall live on in my child, Claude. It is natural to feel this is an end, but as the Buddha taught us, there is no self. Does a wave die when it breaks?” and so on.

There’s a mural by Diego Rivera I love. It’s called Man, Controller of the Universe :

It’s a collage of images of science, technology, history, cells, galaxies, the universe at the nanoscale and the exascale. And at the center there is a man, his hands grasping the controls. He wears a complicated expression: the weight of responsibility for the future, the weight of autonomy.

And I see this mural, and think: how great is Man! Our life is like a breath of air, we were beset by illness and hunger and cold, millions and hundreds of millions died in plagues. And yet we—sick, hungry, short-lived—learned the system of the world, crawled out of the caves, brought nature to heel, walked on the Moon. The last shall be first! And eyes that are clouded with age have seen the furthest stars, and the lives of a cell, and the worlds of Cantor and Hilbert: the invisible world that waited forever. We are dust and ashes, and yet our minds bestride the universe. How great is Man!

And when I read the Riemann announcement, when I read Machines of Loving Grace : humanity is not at the center. Claude is at the center. We are hidden in the margins, passive recipients of manna from Claude. How great is Claude! How noble in reason, how infinite in benevolence! The dancing star, the living word !

It’s a betrayal and a surrender. Man is a bridge , a rusty old bridge that we can neither preserve nor restore . We can move forward and become as the gods, or retreat back into the caves. And the dream of the AI companies, and of most people in AI safety and effective altruism and rationalism ; is instead that we should lie down in a warm bath, watch the demons we summoned dance in the sky, and slip away. Why live? Our servants can do that for us . Why should we explore, discover, invent, succeed, become more, struggle, win, become divine? We don’t want to be more . We don’t want anything.

items.title: A new Nepal, an old neighbour - Balendra Shah's India test
items.summary: Trade, connectivity and regional cooperation will be on top of the agenda when Nepal's PM meets his India counterpart.
items.content:
Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah's visit to India has raised hopes of a reset, marking the first high-level engagement between leaders of Nepal's new political generation and its giant neighbour.

It is Shah's first bilateral visit since his Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) swept to power in March, six months after a Gen Z uprising against corruption and nepotism toppled K P Sharma Oli's government.

The 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician arrives in Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit, during which he will meet his Indian counterpart Narendra Modi and other senior officials.

The talks are expected to cover a broad range of issues, including economic and energy cooperation, the opening of new air corridors, and a reconstruction assistance package following the devastating flash floods that struck Nepal in August.

The disaster killed more than 1,450 in the Himalayan nation, while thousands remain missing and unaccounted for.

India and Nepal share close ethnic, cultural, religious and economic ties, with a largely open border stretching more than 1,750km (1,080 miles).

Wedged between India and China, Nepal is a strategic buffer and, analysts say, its stability has direct implications for India's security.

But over the decades the relationship has been strained by territorial disputes, allegations of political interference and resentment over what many in Nepal see as the dominant 'Big Brother' attitude of Delhi.

Nevertheless, analysts see Shah's visit as an opportunity for a reset.

"The new Nepali leadership says they do not have the political baggage of the past and they want to focus on development, diplomacy and economic partnership," Ranjit Rae, a former Indian ambassador to Nepal tells BBC.

"They seem to be more pragmatic, less ideological. I personally feel it's an optimistic moment," he adds.

Since Nepal abolished monarchy and became a democratic republic in 2008 three political parties dominated the governance.

Delhi has maintained close contacts with all of them – the Communist Party of Nepal (CPN – UML), the Nepali Congress and the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist Centre).

Nepal's communist parties were seen as closer to India's rival China, owing to ideological ties, and often criticised Delhi over what they viewed as unequal bilateral agreements.

Due to Nepal's strategic location, both Delhi and Beijing compete for influence in Kathmandu, leading to accusations the two Asian giants are meddling in the internal affairs of Nepal.

But Nepal's ties with India extend beyond diplomacy and strategic interests.

The Hindu-majority nations share deep social ties, with families straddling the open border and communities interacting daily.

Bilateral trade exceeds $9bn, heavily skewed in India's favour - a longstanding source of resentment in Kathmandu. India is also Nepal's main supplier of petroleum products and several food items, and a key transit route for its trade with the rest of the world.

One key area of co-operation is hydropower. India has approved projects to import up to 1,200MW of electricity from Nepal and is looking to expand imports further.

"India has a huge demand for electricity and Nepal has the potential to generate due to its water resources and geography. It's not just bilateral, Nepal also exports electricity to Bangladesh via India," says Rae.

India has often been among the first countries to assist Nepal during major natural disasters, including the 2015 earthquake and the flash floods in August this year.

Despite the close links, Nepal and India have their differences.

In 2019, Nepal was furious after India published a map that included areas claimed by Kathmandu, in a western region close to the border with China, as part of its territory. That raised heightened awareness in Kathmandu about the region.

The diplomatic wrangle escalated after Nepal published its own map which included those disputed areas.

"I hope Nepal's prime minister raises the border issue with Delhi this time. There may not be a resolution immediately, but they should start negotiations to settle the issue," Kanak Mani Dixit, a veteran Nepali political analyst, told the BBC.

Nepal has also long urged India to open additional air entry routes, allowing large aircraft to fly in from the west to its new airports at Bhairahawa, near the Buddhist holy site of Lumbini, and Pokhara, a major tourist destination.

Access to Indian airspace would mean shorter flights at lower cost and, with more flights, the airports would become commercially viable.

Some in Nepal also believe that Delhi is wary of the fact that the Gautam Buddha international airport was constructed by China's Northwest Civil Aviation Airport and the airport in Pokhara was built with Chinese financial assistance .

Shah has yet to make any overtures to Beijing, but sent a 20-member delegation of party MPs to China for an 11-day visit from 15 November, ahead of his trip to India - seen as an effort to balance ties with Nepal's two powerful neighbours.

Shah had pledged not to travel abroad during his first year in office, but devastating flash floods in August have changed the calculus.

His government estimates reconstruction will cost nearly $5bn, while international aid pledged so far has fallen short of expectations.

But some observers in Nepal believe that Shah's preparations for the high-stake India visit have been less than thorough.

"Prime Minister Shah and his advisors are young and fresh, but they do lack experience. Repeatedly they have exhibited a lack of gravitas in governance, which would be essential for diplomacy with an overwhelmingly powerful neighbour," says Dixit.

Shah is already facing criticism over some of his government's recent decisions, including to remove police chief Dan Bahadur from his post after he allegedly refused to comply with directives from the Prime Minister's office.

Police were sent to some news organisations to detain journalists for their news coverage triggering accusations of curtailing press freedom.

While Kathmandu has ambitions in advancing its ties with India, the real test for Shah would be to return home with tangible outcomes. Securing concrete commitments from Delhi on financial aid would be seen as a diplomatic success and could help blunt growing domestic criticism.

items.title: Dead pets were meant to be cremated - then their bodies appeared on a livestream
items.summary: Grieving Filipinos confront a distressing reality: their dogs and cats may not have received the send-off they paid for.
items.content:
A man – bald, goateed, wearing red-tinted sunglasses – walks down a cracked back road, guiding the camera towards a cluster of plastic-wrapped objects that spill out of the tall grass.

Names are written on the packages – Brandon; Ira; Lucky; Sweet – and numbers. One says 29kg (4.5 stone). Another says 2.5kg. Through the plastic you can make out what appears to be fur, claws and a flattened ear.

It's a mass dumping, the man explains. "We have about 25 animals here that have been dumped in bags. A couple of cats, some dogs."

Warning: This story contains images some might find upsetting

In the weeks since that video was streamed on Facebook, Chris and Geraldine Taylor, who run animal rescue NGO Luna and Furry Siblings (LAFS), say they have uncovered 15 dumping sites in the suburbs of Bulacan, near the Philippines' capital of Manila.

In total they've unearthed the remains of some 170 dead pets. Belgian Malinois, golden retrievers, pugs, puppies and cats have been found dumped off service roads, sealed in septic tanks, floating in rivers and buried in vacant lots.

Many of these animals are thought to have been sent to cremation businesses in the expectation they would be turned to ash.

Now, many grieving owners are having to confront a distressing reality: their beloved pets may not have received the send-off they paid for. The urn in their home may not contain their pet at all. And they may in fact see their so-called fur child again, jettisoned like common waste on the side of a highway.

One saw the livestream and wrote on Facebook: "I think one of those pets is mine." Below, they attached a photo of a beaming Alsatian.

When Chris arrived on that back road three weeks ago, he couldn't have known he was uncorking a scandal that would see at least one business reportedly shut, four people placed under investigation, and a personal invite to sit down with a senator to discuss animal-cruelty laws.

Chris, a former police officer, and his wife are retired, but only formally. For the past three years, they've been running an animal rescue shelter out of their home in San Jose del Monte, 30km (18.6 miles) north-east of central Manila.

On 30 October, he'd driven into town to report a case of animal neglect at the local district office. When he arrived, he was told the official in charge had just left to respond to another complaint: a report of dumped animals on a nearby roadside.

Chris had seen this once before: 14 dogs that were found and soon reburied. This time, he followed the official to the scene and started documenting – taking photos, scanning the bodies for microchips and uploading footage to his Facebook page.

"I figured there's got to be more to this," he explains. "So we put out word: if anybody knows anything, any other dump locations... just report it. Let us know."

In the days that followed, tip-offs started trickling in. More dumpsites emerged.

"The long vacant lot on the left side... that's where the smell comes from," read one message.

"When we ran to this place it smelled of rotting animals," read another, accompanied by a photo of a map with a location circled in red.

By crowdsourcing intel in this way, and collaborating with authorities, LAFS has so far uncovered a total of 15 dumpsites, containing an estimated 170 animals. "Some of them were just bags of bones," Chris says. "Others were liquefied."

LAFS has meticulously documented the crime scenes. Often wearing little more for protection than an N95 mask and rubber gloves, Chris crouches in the underbrush and slices open discarded plastic bags, picking through the contents while Geraldine holds the camera.

Their Facebook videos have racked up more than 30 million views. Commenters ask Chris if he has seen their pet among the bodies, or if he can turn a carcass over so they can check for identifying marks.

Some are successful. On that first night in October, all 25 bodies were returned to their owners.

There's a question which hangs uncomfortably over every dumpsite: who would do something like this?

As more owners came forward, a common denominator emerged. Many said they'd taken the animals to be incinerated at the same place: a crematorium called Ahjay Paws in the city of Bacoor, not far from Manila.

"So I posted: anybody that's had Ahjay's services... these might be your animals," says Chris. "And man, it just flooded in."

The Philippines has long been a dog-loving nation, but since the Covid-19 pandemic the "fur parenting" community has exploded.

A 2021 study found the country had the highest rate of dog ownership in the Asia-Pacific. Since then, the pet dog population has increased 4.7% year on year, according to another study, exceeding 21 million in 2025.

As the numbers soar, businesses have stepped up to address an inevitable implication: more deaths.

"Cremation here in the Philippines has become quite a big thing with the boom of the pet industry," says Anna Cabrera, director at the Philippine Animal Welfare Society (Paws). "There's even a ceremony where they hold wakes for the pets."

These events offer grieving owners a last chance to see their beloved pets before they're taken to a crematorium and transmuted into an urnful of ashes.

Revecca Calling, who lives south of Bulacan in the city of Cavite, says she paid Ahjay Paws 8,500 Philippine pesos (£100; $133) to cremate her dog Olaf in January. The price was calculated according to weight, and included a 30-minute viewing where she could say her final goodbye.

Calling says Ahjay Paws told her they couldn't record the cremation, as it might endanger the staff. They took away Olaf's body, and a few days later handed back a small urn that purportedly contained her cremated remains.

When nine months later Calling heard that dozens of animals' bodies had been found dumped on an empty plot of land, potentially at the behest of a pet cremation business, she was devastated.

"Pet owners entrust these services with something very important: the remains of a beloved family member," she says. "We need to know what happened."

Earlier this month, the Philippines' National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) filed criminal complaints against four individuals in connection with dumped pets. Among them is the owner of Ahjay Paws and two people who ran Bulacan's Pet HPHT Crematory.

According to the NBI, Ahjay Paws had initially arranged to acquire a cremation machine from Pet HPHT – but when it didn't arrive, they opted to send the pet remains to Pet HPHT instead. When the volume of those remains became more than Pet HPHT could handle, that firm paid a third party to bury them.

One interpretation is that the dumping incidents are a result of logistical failures: two businesses that bit off more than they could chew and took desperate measures to make the problem go away.

But there's another theory: that the dead pets could be evidence of a lucrative racket, with people's money taken to incinerate their pets but the animals then being dumped instead.

There is a word for this kind of deception in Philippine law – estafa; where a perpetrator knowingly misleads a victim to financially defraud them – and the NBI say they are investigating it as a possibility in this case.

Two weeks ago, Ahjay Paws' owner denied responsibility for the dumping in San Jose del Monte, according to local media. The company is apparently no longer operating, and the BBC has been unable to contact it.

The BBC has also reached out to Pet HPHT and invited it to respond. On Facebook, the firm said the dumping allegations were "completely false and have no basis".

Another grieving pet owner, Emelia Legada, says she paid Ahjay Paws 10,000 Philippine pesos (£120; $160) to cremate her dog Harvey six months ago.

"I just can't accept the pain of not knowing what might have happened to him," she says. "I really want to confirm whether Harvey was properly cremated, and whether the ashes I received were truly his."

Many are wrestling with the same uncertainty. As Cabrera puts it: "God knows what that was inside those urns."

In response to those anxieties, a veterinarian in nearby Quezon City has started offering complimentary forensic ash testing. For those whose pets have been found among the bodies, other crematoriums have offered to do the job properly, and for free.

The animal welfare society, Paws, is volunteering legal services to help people file complaints with the authorities, and has received more than 150 requests so far. It is also calling for a nationwide audit of all pet cremation businesses.

On 2 November, Percival Vilar Cendaña of the Philippines' progressive Akbayan Party appeared on national television. He was there to speak about the pet-dumping scandal, which, in the span of a few days, had flared into a national disgrace.

"Our worst fears have been confirmed," he told the Bilyonaryo news channel. "Now we see that these are not isolated incidents. It is true that this is a syndicate that is conducting widespread operations."

Neither the police nor the NBI have confirmed that the dumpings were carried out by a "syndicate", nor that they were "widespread". Many details surrounding the case remain murky. But the hysteria is real – and Cendaña was giving voice to a common sentiment.

items.title: Sir Brian May adds new dimension to Hera asteroid
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.esa.int/articles/about-us/directorates/operations/space-safety/hera/sir-brian-may-adds-new-dimension-to-hera-asteroid Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50583768 Points: 54 # Comments: 12
items.content:
Hera science team member, astrophysicist and Queen guitarist Sir Brian May has added an additional dimension to the ESA planetary defence mission’s early views of the Didymos asteroid system via stereoscopic imagery – revealing the dramatic features of this exotic body as never before.

Sir Brian May comments: “The Hera spacecraft acquired these two images on 06 November as it circled the Didymos system at a distance of 29.7 km with a resolution of 2.8 m per pixel, providing the perfect opportunity to create this stereoscopic image. Viewed in depth, the sharpness and smoothness of Didymos’s equatorial ridge is very apparent, compared with the rock-strewn surface of the rest of the asteroid.”

Hera principal investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS / Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur, adds: “Allowing us to observe in 3D with stereo pairs really makes us feel like we are there – even though these images come from 197 million km away. The result is both spectacular and scientifically meaningful.”

Sir Brian May produced this stereoscopic view of Didymos with his colleague Claudia Manzoni. It combines adjacent acquisitions of the asteroid taken a few moments apart using Hera’s main Asteroid Framing Camera instrument by the instrument’s principal investigator Jean-Baptiste Vincent of the German Aerospace Center, DLR .

The very slight changes between the two images mimic the way our two human eyes view the same objects from very slightly different angles to yield stereo vision. The challenge comes in aligning the two images in a manner that seems optically true to our eyes.

The stereoscopic views can be seen using colour 3D glasses, a dedicated viewer or else with your own eyes through ‘free viewing’ .

The 3D view can be seen using a pair of red and blue 3D glasses. The second version can be seen by crossing your eyes, while the third can be accessed by looking into infinity – or else via a dedicated viewer, such as the OWL stereoscope , designed by Sir Brian May and available from the London Stereoscopic Company .

Stereoscopic versions of Hera’s views of Mars moon Deimos acquired during its 2025 flyby of the red planet previously helped guide a simulation-based study of the moon’s violent past history

In 2022 the small moonlet of Didymos called Dimorphos – not seen here – was impacted by NASA’s DART spacecraft to shift its orbit around the larger body. Now the European Space Agency’s Hera mission has arrived to perform a close-up ‘crash scene investigation’ of the binary asteroid system, to gather vital data to turn this grand-scale experiment into a well understood and potentially repeatable planetary defence technique.

Join the Hera team on the evening of Wednesday 25 November as they share the first close-up images of this historic transformed space object.

Our Hera livestream starts from 19:45 to 20:30 CET on Wednesday 25 November. Follow the livestream on ESA WebTV or the ESA YouTube channel .

Subscribe to our newsletter to receive the latest news, mission updates, and exclusive insights directly in your inbox. Be the first to know about our upcoming projects and breakthroughs.

items.title: US declassifies more UFO footage filmed in the Middle East
items.summary: The Pentagon has released an eighth tranche of UFO records, which includes three video clips recorded in 2020, 2023 and 2026.
items.content:
The US government released an eighth tranche of records regarding Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAPs), marking the latest step in an effort to declassify government files on UFOs.

After US President Donald Trump called for UFO files to be released in an executive order earlier this year, the Pentagon has declassified hundreds of files. The first tranche was released 8 May 2026.

The footage in this video makes up three of the 43 files released in this tranche. All three clips were filmed from aboard US military platforms in the Middle East in 2020, 2023 and 2026.

items.title: In a year of AI solving maths problems, Anthropic may have just solved the biggest
items.summary: A mathematician at Anthropic says he used an AI to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis, though verification will take some time.
items.content:
An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.

Levent Alpöge said , external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut , that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.

If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. Alpöge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".

The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.

As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.

It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.

Named for the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.

Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.

Alpöge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.

"The precise timing is horrible," Alpöge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier."

"I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.

The complete textual proof that Alpöge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 pages long.

Terrance Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday , external that verification of the proof is still some way off.

"I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.

No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.

OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.

More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.

The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.

Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths , external and physics , external .

A group of maths scholars said , external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".

"We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.

A month later, OpenAI released , external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.

It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

items.title: Lite tra famiglie finisce nel sangue, donna muore accoltellata a Roma
items.summary: La vittima è una 52enne di etnia rom
items.content:
Una lite tra famiglie è degenerata nel sangue stasera alla periferia di Roma. Una donna di 52 anni è morta dopo essere stata accoltellata. Fermata dai carabinieri la presunta responsabile.

Secondo una prima ricostruzione dei fatti, ancora al vaglio degli inquirenti, quattro donne di etnia Rom residenti in un comune a sud della provincia di Roma avrebbero raggiunto a bordo di un'auto alcune abitazioni in via Fontanile Tuscolano, occupate da altre donne appartenenti allo stesso nucleo familiare allargato. Alla base del gesto vi sarebbero stati pregressi dissidi di natura privata: l'intento del gruppo sarebbe stato quello di appiccare un incendio alle strutture.

A quanto ricostruito, una volta giunte sul posto e dopo aver cosparso di liquido infiammabile l'esterno degli edifici la situazione è rapidamente degenerata in una violenta rissa. Durante la lite la vittima è stata raggiunta da diversi fendenti inferti con un'arma da taglio. Subito dopo l'aggressione, hanno tentato di soccorrere la ferita caricandola a bordo della stessa auto con cui erano arrivate, dirigendosi verso il Policlinico Tor Vergata. La corsa verso l'ospedale si è tuttavia interrotta a causa di un lieve incidente stradale autonomo. La donna è deceduta durante il tragitto. I militari dell'Arma hanno rintracciato e fermato la presunta autrice dell'accoltellamento, insieme alle altre donne coinvolte nella vicenda, le cui posizioni sono attualmente al vaglio dell'Autorità Giudiziaria. Proseguono intanto i rilievi tecnico-scientifici sul luogo dell'aggressione e su quello dell'incidente per definire con esattezza la dinamica dell'accaduto.

items.title: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
items.summary: Pressures weighed on US markets, with the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average pushed into correction territory.
items.content:
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.

The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors.

Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week.

The S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.

The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.

The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.

Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development.

Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.

Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.

Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.

Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.

While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.

"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.

"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."

Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell on Friday as the market sell-off continued.

Nvidia shares had plummeted by 13.7% by the close of trade, following Reuters reports - unconfirmed by the BBC - the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its accounting practices.

Musk's firms Tesla and SpaceX both experienced falls of more than 7.6%. SpaceX shares were hit after it announced a bond sale to finance what the company said was the largest purchase of Nvidia chips on record.

Meta closed down more than 5% and Amazon was down more than 4%, while Apple and Alphabet experienced smaller falls.

Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - also took a hit.

Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower.

Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.

South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.

Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

items.title: French police officers sentenced for beating of music producer Michel Zecler
items.summary: The court has upheld the 2020 beating of the black music producer as an aggravated circumstance of racism.
items.content:
Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.

The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.

Their lies were exposed because the whole scene at Zecler's recording studio was caught on CCTV, revealing the producer had suffered some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance at all.

Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Philippe Tondeux, 50, and Pierre Plantier, 37, all received five year sentences, with different amounts suspended.

Lapersonne had three years of his sentence suspended and Tondeux three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended, and will serve his one year with an ankle monitor.

The case became a cause célèbre for critics of the police, who say it exposed systematic racism among officers. With police again facing criticism for alleged use of excessive force in stopping recent protests, the verdict was hotly awaited by Zecler's supporters.

Much depended in the two-week trial on Zecler's own testimony that the officers called him a racial slur during the beating.

This was denied by the three policemen, who in court admitted the beating and the faked report but denied there was a racial motivation. But the court preferred the evidence of the producer, because - unlike the police - everything else he said was verifiably true.

Because the racist element was accepted by the court, the sentences were toughened.

The incident took place during the Covid lockdown in 2020. Zecler was accused by the officers for not wearing a mask when doing so was obligatory as he approached his studio on foot.

They later claimed his behaviour aroused their suspicions, and they thought he might be carrying drugs. No evidence of this emerged.

After Zecler entered the lobby, the police followed - without a warrant - and tried to bring him outside. Zecler refused to go out, and the beating ensued. Zecler cried for help and some people appeared from the basement and pushed the police outside.

The officers then smashed a glass pane and sent a tear-gas grenade into the building, forcing those inside to come out - after which Zecler was again hit. He was then arrested.

During the trial Zecler said had it not been for the CCTV video, he would have been in court not as a victim but as a potential criminal.

In their last words before the court, all three police officers apologised for what they had done. Tondeux said he was sorry "for the image of the police that I have given".

You are now able to stream all of your favorite NIN live recordings from 1988-2026. I can't believe how far the site has come in the last year. Some truly incredible work. Login with your discord account and you can save your favorite recordings to stream and keep your faves organized. As always, feedback is always welcome. Reach out via email if you have comments/suggestions about it.

I am currently adding all of the ticket stubs, setlist scans, passes that I have for each show. Please get in contact if you have anything to contribute. I am also looking for photos from past shows. If you are a photographer and would like to contribute some highlights, I'd love to add them to the archive with a link directed to your site of choice.

Other than that. A few tapes trickling in and I do have some that I am slowly working on. None that are insane upgrades. But would need some work and comparison of previous versions. Notably, I have a 1st gen cassette of the 07/12/1991 NOLA Tipitina's show that sounds killer. I recently transferred the elusive collection of acc123456 and have a queue of VHS/Cassette transfers to check over. I also just finished a 200 DAT tape project for a fellow taper out of NYC. The transfer backlog is clear, for the first time in a while. So if you need anything transferred, or have some old NIN hanging around that isn't on the archive. Email us!

items.title: 'I tell my son it's just fireworks': Life inside Yemeni city besieged by Houthis
items.summary: Orla Guerin speaks to seven people trapped in the key city of Taiz, cut off from the outside world for weeks.
items.content:
In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie.

"When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she says. "I don't want him to panic, but deep down I know he is old enough to understand what is happening around him. He has lived through war for most of his life."

Taiz has long been a prize - and a front line - in Yemen's civil war.

Houthi forces tightened their grip last month, fully encircling the government-controlled city, and the population - estimated to be between 600,000 and 1 million.

Since then, Yemen's third-largest city has been cut off from the world, and its residents have been largely unheard. We reached seven people inside the city who mapped out the anatomy of the siege.

They gave detailed accounts of the Houthis' death grip on Taiz. Only a minimal amount of food can get in. Prices for staples like rice, sugar and cooking oil have doubled or even trebled. Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling.

On streets that used to hum with traffic and background chatter, a silence has fallen. Schools are closed and restaurants are shuttered. Suffering is being heaped on suffering. Piles of rubbish are trapped inside the city, alongside the people. When residents try to get rid of it by burning it, there is a toxic smoke. Even the air is now a Houthi weapon.

From positions on the hills, rebel fighters - and snipers - can wage war on the city below.

Estimates for the death toll vary widely. At the Office for Siege Affairs, a local government department, they say 148 civilians have been killed by Houthi attacks since August.

Some of those we contacted in Taiz do not want to be identified because they fear for their safety. Many in the city are reluctant to even speak on the phone because the Houthis control key mobile carriers.

"Sometimes it feels like the city has become a huge prison," says Ashwaq, a teacher and mother of three, who only wanted her first name to be used. She yearns for the old Taiz.

"It used to be a lively city," she says. "People loved life, worked hard, visited one another, and had hopes for the future, despite all the difficulties. Now, we hardly go out anymore. The [Houthi] shelling can happen any time, and sniper fire near the front lines makes even a short trip dangerous."

"I worry about them every single day, every hour, and honestly every minute," she says.

War is not new to Taiz. The strategic city is the gateway to Aden - the temporary seat of the internationally recognised government - and to southern Yemen.

Houthi rebels - backed by Iran - reached the outskirts of Taiz in 2015, cutting off roads, and laying siege from three sides. A year earlier, they had seized Yemen's capital, Sanaa.

More than a decade on, the government, which is weak and fractured, has been unable to reclaim the capital and much of north-western Yemen. That's despite the backing of Saudi Arabia, and its air strikes.

In recent months, the conflict has flared up and expanded after a four-year lull. The Houthis made a lightning advance, taking territory from the government, and striking Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones.

A long-running civil war has become a threat to regional stability.

An emergency room doctor, whom we are calling Yaser, bears witness to that.

Among the war wounded recently brought to his hospital were four children, shot by Houthi snipers. They usually aim for the head and chest, he tells us. Two of the four children died.

The hardest thing he faces, as a father himself, is treating wounded children. "I have to rise to the responsibility, compose myself and support the families," he says. "It's a difficult situation that I cannot even put into words, when I see a father looking at his badly wounded child right in front of him."

Most of the injured are victims of shelling. Reaching the hospital can be an ordeal. Some families have to walk for hours from outlying areas.

They arrive exhausted, like the doctors who will treat them, and who are struggling with "everything", says Yaser. Even sterilising fluid for surgical instruments is in short supply.

He tells us the hospital is running on empty, and can carry on for two more weeks, "maybe".

"Funerals heading to the cemeteries have become the defining scene in Taiz, around the clock," says Taiz's Governor, Nabil Shamsan.

"The people of Taiz are losing their lives due to supply shortages, lack of food, and loss of income," he says. "Every single day, we bury dozens of Taiz residents."

We have not been able to independently verify these figures.

He remains inside the city, and inside the siege. "I live among my people," he says.

On a video call, he looks weary but delivers a lengthy chronicle of a city being starved of oxygen - literally.

He tells us that hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity, and 120 health centres have closed. Diseases are spreading, neonatal deaths have increased, and malnutrition is surging. Hundreds of kidney patients are not getting dialysis because they can't get to hospitals or because fuel is short when they do.

The Houthi leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, has denied Taiz is besieged. Late last month, he claimed that routes remained open for food, medicine and humanitarian aid.

That is denied by the government, residents of Taiz, aid agencies and the United Nations.

What's at stake in the battle for the city is more than territory, says Shamsan.

He says the Houthis - who mostly follow a branch of Shia Islam - want to change the character of this predominantly Sunni city, long known as a seat of learning and a bastion of resistance.

"Everyone knows that Taiz is a hub of culture, a city characterised by freedom, political pluralism and all forms of civic life," he says. In sharp contrast, he says, the Houthis aim to impose their strict religious doctrine and drag the city "back to the dark ages".

Whatever the pressure on the city and its people, the governor insists the Houthis will never win.

They are defending their city, alongside relatives, friends, neighbours, and five brigades of pro-government troops, who can't do the job on their own.

They don't have heavy weapons or enough numbers for the expanding front line.

Training camps have sprung up for volunteers, but the lessons can be as brief as a day or two before they are sent to join the fight.

Akram (not his real name) is already a veteran. He's 31, with a child on the way.

When Taiz was fully encircled before, in 2015, he broke away from his studies and took up arms. In that round of fighting, the Houthis gained control of his district on the outskirts, and he was uprooted. He hasn't seen his old home since then.

Last month, when Taiz was completely cut off once again, he bought a rifle, paying about $1,200 (£910) for a Chinese version of a Kalashnikov. It used to cost less than half that sum.

"This time the Houthis have new technology and new missiles," he says. "They can wage a war in the air with drones. We fear the death of our families and our civilians, and ourselves."

He has already lost four friends in the past month, who left behind wives and children.

But Akram, and many others, see defending Taiz as their duty. He says that "all the sons of Taiz" will fight the Houthis "and their extremism".

The armed group is currently designated as a foreign terrorist organisation by the US (which has gone back and forth on the issue) but not by the UK or the European Union.

"They say God gave them the right to rule everyone in Yemen. We don't accept that," says Akram. "We live in freedom. We cannot surrender; we cannot leave. We cannot breathe without our city."

But it can be suffocating inside Taiz, where nightfall brings no rest.

"Every night we have bombing and shelling," says Ahmad Al-Basha, a photographer. "I think the Houthis prefer to fight at night. Maybe they don't want us and our children to sleep inside our homes."

The people of Taiz feel let down, he tells us, by their government and by the international community. "We feel frustrated and sad," he says, "because we don't see any move to help us."

Many believe the Houthis will keep a chokehold on Taiz from the outside, and exert significant control over the city without trying to enter it.

Ahmad believes it won't come to that but fears the worst if it does.

"Maybe they will clean Taiz of any resistance, kill people and settle scores with anyone who is against them," he says.

His greatest concern is for his children, who cannot escape the sounds of war.

"I tell them it's a party," he says, "and if it's really loud, I say it's a big party."

As Taiz endures bombing, shelling, and a sense of abandonment laced with growing hunger, Ashwaq has a parent's plea for the international community.

"Please don't forget Taiz," she says. "We are ordinary families. We want our children to study, play and dream like other children around the world. We are not just numbers in news reports."

On Yemen's desert battlefield, a war with global consequences is being waged

items.title: Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper
items.summary: The Russian embassy in Denmark has denied the allegation, which has led to Russia's defence attaché being expelled.
items.content:
Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "initiated" the attempt.

Denmark's security and intelligence agency said it had stopped individuals who were intending to kill the person, named by Danish media as rapper Kyivstoner, at a concert in September. Two people were charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service, and pleaded not guilty.

Denmark's foreign minister said Russia's defence attaché will now be expelled.

Russia's Embassy in Denmark called the allegations "unsubstantiated" and said Copenhagen failed to provide evidence of Moscow's involvement.

In a statement posted on social media, the embassy claimed a "Danish model" had emerged, which it described as a "Russian trace" allegedly being discovered and "exploited for a propaganda spectacle". It accused Denmark of "provocations" intending to "frighten the Danish population in order to justify... a prolonged confrontation with Russia".

Russian state media cites the foreign ministry in Moscow as saying it will respond to the expulsion of its official "accordingly".

Danish media named the target of the assassination attempt as the rapper known as Kyivstoner, whose real name is Albert Vasiliev.

Denmark's security and intelligence agency (PET) said the individuals who allegedly tried to assassinate him were associated with a banned Danish gang named Loyal to Familia. The group is "known for extensive, serious and violent criminal activity", according to the agency.

PET, which worked with police on the case, said three individuals were stopped while travelling by car near the music venue where Kyivstoner was set to perform on 25 September.

Since then, two people linked to the case have been charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service.

Both individuals pleaded not guilty to the charges, local media reported.

In July, Russia's FSB security service accused Vasiliev and the Ukrainian authorities of organising a "terrorist attack" on military facilities and personnel in Russia. The rapper denied this allegation on social media.

In a statement on Friday, Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said the alleged assassination attempt was Russian "intimidation" and an attempt to make Denmark "waver" in its support for Ukraine.

Russia's defence attaché must leave the country within seven days, Rasmussen said.

He also said Denmark wants the EU to restrict the ability of Russians to travel throughout Europe, saying even though Denmark is already very reluctant to issue visas, Russians can still get a Schenegen visa in another country and travel to Denmark. Denmark wants these visas to apply only in the country that has issued them, he added.

items.title: What the new UK-EU deal could mean for future post-Brexit relations
items.summary: The BBC's political and Europe editors analyse the new agreements between the UK and EU.
items.content:
The United Kingdom and European Union reached a deal on Friday strengthening post-Brexit ties following a summit in Brussels.

The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, while European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK.

The BBC's political editor Chris Mason and Europe editor Katya Adler analyse the new agreement and what it could mean for future relations between the UK and EU.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".
